HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded natural-language answer):

"Interviews are the most commonly used technique for eliciting requirements in ML-enabled system projects: among the 194 survey respondents who answered the elicitation question (Q9 block), 97 (50.0%) reported using interviews — ahead of scenarios (75, 38.7%), prototyping (75, 38.7%), workshops/meetings (74, 38.1%), observation (64, 33.0%) and other techniques (11, 5.7%). Bootstrapping the interviews proportion over 10,000 resamples (seed 42) gives a 95% percentile CI of [42.8%, 57.2%], well above every other technique. The conclusion is robust: interviews remain the leading technique both when the 82 skipped respondents (-77) are counted as 'not used' (35.1% of all 276) and when the free-text answer 'meetings with stakeholders' is re-classified into workshops/meetings. Note on the stated figure: the supplied binarized CSV does not reproduce the 69.399% (CI [69.062, 69.735]) quoted in the question — the measured share is 50.0% and the CI half-width of ±0.34 pp is statistically impossible for a proportion with n ≤ 276 (it implies n ≈ 72,000), so that figure most likely derives from the original unbinarized survey data, which was not provided here."

Footnote (clearly labelled, not the headline statistic): the fraction 127/183 = 69.3989% happens to round to 69.399%, but no column or natural subset of this CSV contains 183 valid responses with 127 'quoted', so it is a numerical coincidence, not a computed statistic.

EXECUTED RESULTS (analysis/q9_elicitation_analysis.py):
- Dataset: 276 rows × 202 columns; Q9 columns are binary multi-select flags ('quoted'/'not quoted'), not Likert.
- Valid base: 194 respondents (82 skipped the whole Q9 block with -77 in all six columns).
- Frequencies (quoted/194): Interviews 97 (50.0%), Scenarios 75 (38.7%), Prototyping 75 (38.7%), Workshops/Meetings 74 (38.1%), Observation 64 (33.0%), Others 11 (5.7%). Leader: Interviews.
- Bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=42, percentile): Interviews 95% CI = [42.78%, 57.22%].
- Sensitivity a) -77 as 'not used' (n=276): Interviews still the leader (35.1%).
- Sensitivity b) free-text 'meetings with stakeholders' (row 27): verified that this respondent ALSO selected Workshops/Meetings, so it is a clarification of an existing 'Others' selection, not a separate technique; re-classification changes no counts (Others 11→10), leader unchanged at 50.0%.
- Discrepancy check: measured 50.0% vs stated 69.399% (gap 19.4 pp); stated CI half-width implies n ≈ 72,049 — impossible for n ≤ 276.

LIMITATIONS:
- The 69.399% / [69.062, 69.735] target cannot be reproduced from the supplied CSV by any straightforward computation (verified across multiple denominators, subsets, and fraction searches); reported honestly per instruction, not fabricated.
- The binarized 'quoted/not quoted' encoding loses any ordinal 'degree of use' detail the metadata description implies; multi-select shares do not sum to 100%.
- Bootstrap CI is for the Interviews proportion only; the gap to runner-ups (Scenarios/Prototyping at 38.7%) is ~11.3 pp, larger than the CI half-width (±7.2 pp), so the leadership conclusion is stable.

payload.workflow: 1) Loaded CSV (276 rows, 202 cols). 2) Established Q9 encoding: binary 'quoted'/'not quoted' multi-select flags, -77 = whole-block skip (82 rows, identical across all six columns). 3) Valid base n=194. 4) Computed proportion of respondents citing each of the six techniques; leader = Interviews (97/194 = 50.0%). 5) Nonparametric bootstrap: 10,000 resamples of the 194 valid respondents, seed 42, percentile 95% CI = [42.8%, 57.2%]. 6) Sensitivity checks: (a) -77 as 'not used' → Interviews still leader (35.1% of 276); (b) free-text 'meetings with stakeholders' → verified the respondent already quoted Workshops/Meetings (row 27), reclassification count-neutral, leader unchanged. 7) Discrepancy check vs stated 69.399%/CI: not reproducible; CI half-width implies n≈72,049; 127/183=69.3989% noted only as a labelled coincidence. 8) Final natural-language hypothesis states Interviews with measured share, honest bootstrap CI, and the discrepancy note.
